source.title: Relative Generalization Invariance of LLM Pretraining
source.authors: Feng-Zhuo Zhang; Shu-Che Wang; Sheng-Gui Li; Tian-Yu Ruan; Jian-Liang He; I. Tsang; Tian-Yu Pang; Chao Du; Tian-Wei Zhang; Zhuo-Ran Yang

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling-law work in its related-work discussion but does not test or rely on the claim's power-law fits or compute-optimal allocation. Its experiments concern relative generalization invariance, a related but different property of token-wise validation losses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own held-out-loss experiments, but measures whether loss differences between tokens are preserved across training runs (RGI), not power-law scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, or the absolute size of architecture-induced loss changes. The RGI results are recorded as findings outside the listed claim versions. Scaling-law results mentioned only as prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. appear only in related work. The experiments measure relative generalization invariance (RGI): whether token-wise validation-loss differences are preserved across optimizers, architectures and data streams. The paper fits no power law in parameters, tokens or compute. It makes no extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation, reports no downstream tasks, and does not compare absolute loss across shapes at fixed parameter count. The 124M, 0.7B and 4.5B runs only check that RGI persists, not how loss scales.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. One addition: the authors also prove that RGI emerges in an overparameterized quadratic model across GD, Adam and Muon, with parameter cosine similarity falling over training.
record.recipe_differences: The study defines and evaluates relative generalization invariance using token-wise validation-loss comparisons; it does not implement the scaling-law measurement or fitting procedure in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: RGI varies with training data stream, validation distribution, model width, initialization, and optimizer hyperparameters; hyperparameters affect when RGI emerges.

fits_no_version.finding: Across six optimizers with shared initialization and FineWeb stream, token-wise validation losses differ by a near-constant shift after about 2,000 steps (rCCC > 0.95, rdiff < 0.05; linear fits with R² ≥ 0.99). This persists at 0.7B and 4.5B for Adam vs Muon.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice shifts token-wise validation loss approximately uniformly, preserving relative token-loss structure.

fits_no_version.finding: RGI holds across independent initializations, widths 768 vs 384, and attention and FFN variants, but fails between widths 768 and 64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moderate architecture changes preserve relative token-loss structure; large width reductions do not.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on ArXiv or CodeParrot instead of FineWeb prevents RGI. C4 gives a non-monotonic rCCC. Validation on random tokens shows no RGI.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative generalization structure is set mainly by the training data stream and the validation distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: RGI coexists with large movement of parameters and hidden states away from initialization and with low cross-optimizer similarity. It persists at width 192, which falls outside the apparent mean-field regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RGI is not explained by the NTK or mean-field regimes alone.

record.problems: The reported evidence concerns RGI rather than the scaling-law versions in the claim. Many outcomes are described qualitatively or shown only in figures; numerical error bars or confidence intervals are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional optimizer-hyperparameter ablations, alternative baselines, single-token evaluations, and appendix plots for rdiff/rCCC. These were not expanded into separate rows because they repeat the RGI finding across settings and do not test a listed claim version. It also reports quadratic-model theory and auxiliary analyses of loss decomposition and convergence speed, which do not measure the scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: All: no loss-vs-parameters, tokens or compute power-law fit.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: no compute-optimal parameter or token allocation.
All: architecture variants are compared only on relative token-loss structure (rCCC, rdiff), not on absolute loss at fixed parameter count.
All: text LM pretraining only, with no power-law fits in other regimes.
All: no scaling exponents fitted, so no dependence on fitting choices is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Not a scaling-law study. Loss-vs-scale numbers (Table 3 loss gaps, the 124M/0.7B/4.5B runs) are not used to fit or test scaling laws, so no row bears on V1–V7.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as a function of compute.
The paper compares relative token-loss structure across architectures, but does not test whether absolute loss changes only slightly at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices and setup.

rows.value: rdiff < 0.05 after 2,000 steps for all five other optimizers

rows.note: The paper reports the threshold for all five comparators as a group; it does not provide separate numerical values in the text.

rows.subject: 124M Nano-GPT models trained with different optimizers
rows.operation_detail: Compared parameter and hidden-state cosine similarity between initialization and later checkpoints.

conditions.value: Within each optimizer, initialization versus later training steps

rows.measure: Cosine similarity of parameters and hidden states
rows.value: Both parameters and hidden states deviate substantially from initialization.
rows.uncertainty: Averaged over layers, validation examples, and random seeds; no error bars stated.
rows.note: This is evidence discussed in relation to explanations of RGI, not a test of the listed scaling-law versions.

rows.subject: 124M Nano-GPT models trained with different optimizers
rows.operation_detail: Compared parameter and hidden-state cosine similarity across optimizers at matched steps.

conditions.value: Adam versus Adam-mini, Lion, Muon, Soap, or Scion

rows.measure: Cosine similarity of parameters and hidden states
rows.baseline: Adam at the same training step
rows.value: Both similarities decrease as training proceeds; the paper describes the learned features as distinct.
rows.uncertainty: Averaged over layers, validation examples, and random seeds; no error bars stated.
rows.note: This result is used to argue that RGI does not require different optimizers to converge to shared parameters or representations.

rows.subject: 124M Nano-GPT models with widths 768, 576, 384, and 192
rows.operation_detail: Compared relative validation-loss patterns across optimizers at each fixed width.

conditions.value: Adam, Adam-mini, Lion, Muon, Soap, Scion

rows.value: Approximate RGI persists at width 192, one quarter of the standard GPT-2 width; figure only
rows.note: The text states that RGI persists at all tested widths.

rows.subject: Adam-trained 124M Nano-GPT models with widths 768, 576, 384, and 192
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across learning rates and widths after 10,000 steps.
rows.measure: Validation loss as a function of learning rate
rows.value: The width-192 model has a qualitatively different validation-loss–learning-rate profile from the width-768, 576, and 384 models.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that width 192 is not described by the same MF-style approximation.
